shots.words: North Korea built a torpedo they believed no one could trace. They used it to cut a
1,200-ton South Korean warship in half on
an ordinary spring evening. Forty-six of the 104 crew didn't
survive. Then divers went to the seabed
and found the weapon's propulsion section. And
on it was a handwritten marking in Korean that the
five-nation investigation said traced the torpedo back to its maker.
What you are watching
is simulated footage, rebuilt from the documented record.
ROKS Cheonan was a 1,200-ton Pohang-class corvette, commissioned in 1989 and built for coastal patrol
and
anti-submarine warfare. Her hull number was PCC-772,
and on the evening of 26 March 2010 she was doing exactly what she was built to
do. She was on routine patrol near Baengnyeong Island in the Yellow Sea,
a small chunk of rock that sits just below the
Northern Limit Line,
roughly fifteen kilometers off the North Korean coast.
Baengnyeong Island is one of the closest South Korean territories to North Korean
soil,
and the waters around it are shallow, cluttered, and acoustically complex. The seabed is uneven,
the currents shift quickly,
and the underwater terrain
creates false echoes that can mask a real contact or mimic one where
nothing exists. It's an environment that rewards patience
and punishes complacency,
and on this evening the sea offered no warning that anything had changed.
The Northern Limit Line is the disputed maritime boundary where South
and North Korean naval forces have clashed
before. It was drawn by the United Nations Command at the end of the Korean War,
but
North Korea has never accepted it, and both navies treat the waters around it
as contested space. Skirmishes have occurred here in 1999, 2002,
and each time the clashes were brief, violent,
and inconclusive. The South Korean Navy keeps a constant presence in the area to
enforce its claim,
and Cheonan was part of that patrol rotation on 26 March.
One hundred four crew were aboard,
and the watch was
set for a normal night at sea. The ship was moving at cruising
speed, the sensors were operating,
and the weather was calm. There
was no indication that anything was different about this evening,
no warning that the routine itself was about to become the story. Because
in waters like these,
the threat isn't always visible on the surface,
and a ship built to hunt submarines can still be hunted by
one.
The Pohang class was designed for exactly this environment,
shallow coastal waters where larger vessels cannot maneuver effectively. But that same shallow water
that made Cheonan
useful also made her vulnerable. A submarine one-tenth her size could hide in the acoustic clutter near
the bottom,
and on
26 March the acoustic picture was quiet enough that no one on board suspected what
was moving beneath them. They wouldn't find out until
twenty-one twenty-two.
At nine twenty-two that evening, Korean time,
an external underwater explosion tore through the stern of ROKS Cheonan. The blast wasn't internal,
wasn't a mechanical failure,
and wasn't a collision with another surface vessel. It was an external force that struck the ship
from below, and
in seconds the 1,200-ton corvette broke in two.
The forward section stayed afloat long enough for rescue efforts to begin,
but the stern sank
almost immediately. Sailors who were below decks at the moment of impact had
no time to react, and those who survived did so
because
they were on deck or near an escape route. In the chaos of the first minutes,
no one on the scene knew what had
caused the blast. The initial reports suggested everything from
a mine strike to an internal ammunition accident,
because the idea that an enemy submarine
had penetrated South Korean waters undetected was almost too stark
to accept. But the damage was too precise for an accident
and too
focused for a drifting mine.
Fifty-eight crew members were pulled from the water or rescued from the floating bow section. Forty-six sailors
were lost,
and the search for survivors continued through the night
as the stern settled on the seabed. Rescue helicopters circled the area,
lowering divers into
the dark water to search compartments that were already flooding. The temperature was cold,
the current was strong,
and the chances of finding anyone
alive in the sunken stern dropped with every minute.
The ship was gone,
and the question was only beginning. No one knew what weapon
could cut a modern warship in
half without warning, or what force had the skill to deliver it.
The location mattered as much
as
the blast itself. Baengnyeong Island sits just south of the Northern Limit Line,
in waters where North Korean vessels operate regularly
and where the
South Korean Navy expects contact. But contact usually means warning shots and ramming,
not submerged attack without declaration. The scale of the destruction pointed
to something more deliberate than a
mine,
and more precise than an accident. A mine breaks a ship by chance contact. This blast had
been aimed.
In the hours after the explosion,
South Korean naval command faced a choice that would shape everything that followed. They could treat
this
as a tragic accident, which would mean mourning and moving on. Or they could treat it
as an attack, which meant raising
the wreck, investigating the cause,
and risking a military escalation on the Korean peninsula. They chose to raise the ship.
The wreck of ROKS
Cheonan came to rest on the seabed roughly 45 meters below the surface,
and the South Korean military immediately began recovery operations. This wasn't
only a search for bodies
and a rescue of the dead. It was the preservation of evidence,
because a ship that sinks in disputed
waters is a crime scene before it is anything else.
The operation to raise the wreck took weeks,
and it required lifting a broken
1,200-ton warship from the bottom of the Yellow Sea in pieces.
Divers worked in shifts, mapping the debris field, photographing the hull,
and collecting
every fragment that might explain what had happened. The water was murky,
the visibility was poor, and the divers had to work by touch
and torchlight in a debris cloud that had settled over the broken hull.
The stern was raised first,
and when it broke the surface
the damage pattern was already visible to the investigators waiting on
deck. The metal was bent outward, not inward,
which meant the force had
come from outside the hull. The damage wasn't random. It was concentrated
in a specific pattern that suggested a single point of impact from
below,
and the shape of the torn metal matched what naval engineers recognize
as the signature of an underwater explosion directed upward through a
ship's keel. The wreck had become
a message written in steel, and the investigators were learning to read it.
As the salvage teams
worked,
the mission quietly changed from recovery to investigation. Every piece of the wreck was bagged, tagged,
and sent to a secure facility for
analysis,
because the attack had left a physical record in the steel itself. The transformation of a naval
disaster into a forensic scene was
methodical and grim,
and the divers who brought the pieces up knew they were retrieving something more important than steel.
They were retrieving the
story of what had happened at nine twenty-two on 26 March.
The bow section was raised days later,
and when the two halves were
laid out on the dock at Pyeongtaek,
the investigators could see the full geometry of the destruction. The ship hadn't simply flooded. It had
been broken. The gap between the stern
and the bow was clean, as if a giant blade had sliced through the hull,
and the
only force that cuts that cleanly underwater is a bubble-jet torpedo.
South Korea formed the Joint Civilian-Military Investigation Group, a team that included investigators
from the United States,
the United Kingdom, Australia, and Sweden. The inclusion of foreign experts was deliberate,
because any finding that pointed to North
Korea would carry the weight of international legitimacy only if
the evidence was reviewed by eyes outside the South Korean military. Sweden,
in particular,
brought a reputation for neutral forensic rigor,
and its participation was meant to insulate the findings from the charge that Seoul had predetermined
the
outcome.
Forensic teams from the JIG combed through the wreckage
and the damage pattern with precision. They concluded that the explosion was external
and underwater,
which ruled out internal malfunction or surface collision. The blast had occurred below the waterline near the
stern, where the hull was
thickest,
and the force was directed upward through the ship's engineering spaces. This wasn't the random damage of
a drifting mine. It was the
concentrated signature of a torpedo.
The key to understanding the damage was the bubble-jet effect. A bubble-jet torpedo doesn't need to strike
its target
directly. Instead, it detonates beneath the hull, creating a gas bubble that expands
and collapses in a fraction of a second. The collapse generates
a jet of water that punches
upward through the keel with enough force to snap a ship in two. The JIG found evidence
of
this mechanism in the pattern of the broken metal, the distribution of the debris,
and the location of the blast relative to the keel.
Once they saw that signature,
they knew exactly what kind of weapon they were looking for.
As the investigators combed through the debris,
they
found fragments that didn't belong to the ship itself. Small pieces of metal, wire,
and propulsion components were scattered across the seabed near the
wreck,
and some of them bore the design characteristics of a specific class of weapon. Investigators traced the
damage to a CHT-02D torpedo,
a North Korean-built weapon with a bubble-jet design that creates an underwater shockwave capable of breaking a
ship's back without striking it directly.
The
CHT-02D is a wake-homing weapon, which means it tracks the turbulence behind a surface ship
and detonates beneath the stern,
where the hull is
most vulnerable. It's not a fast weapon by modern standards,
but it doesn't need to be fast. It needs to be quiet, patient, and
placed precisely,
and in the shallow waters near Baengnyeong Island, those characteristics were enough.
But the real discovery was still submerged. The investigators knew
that this weapon leaves more than fragments.
It leaves its propulsion section behind,
and if that section could be found, it might carry evidence
that no denial could erase.
Divers recovered the propulsion section of the CHT-02D torpedo from the seabed near the wreck of ROKS
Cheonan,
and
when they brought it to the surface the investigators found something that no simulation had predicted.
On the metal casing of the propulsion unit,
there was a handwritten marking in Korean script. The JIG report described this marking
as a production trace that identified the weapon's manufacturer,
which
meant the torpedo had effectively signed its maker's name on the seabed.
North Korea had built a weapon they assumed would be lost in
the detonation or buried in
the sediment. Instead, the part that survived carried a handwritten marking that survived the blast, the corrosion,
and
the months underwater. The irony was almost architectural. A state that operates in total secrecy had
left a handwritten note on a weapon of
war,
and that note became the single most important piece of evidence in the investigation.
The torpedo was fired from a Yeono-class midget submarine,
a North Korean vessel with a submerged displacement of approximately 130 tons. That means the submarine that
delivered the weapon was roughly one-tenth the
size of the ship it destroyed. The Yeono class is
small enough to operate in the shallow littoral waters near Baengnyeong Island,
where larger
submarines cannot maneuver effectively
and where surface ships have difficulty detecting them against the cluttered acoustic background of the seabed.
The Yeono class is
diesel-electric, which means it runs on batteries when submerged
and surfaces only to recharge. When running on batteries, it's nearly silent,
and its small
size produces a sonar return that can be mistaken for a whale,
a school of fish,
or a patch of rough seabed. Standard anti-submarine
warfare tactics rely on detecting a submarine's propeller noise,
engine vibrations, or hull reflections,
but a 130-ton vessel moving at three knots in shallow
water generates almost none of those signatures.
It is the acoustic equivalent of a shadow,
and on 26 March that shadow moved beneath a
1,200-ton warship without raising a single alarm. The
submarine didn't need to outrun Cheonan. It only needed to outwait her,
and in those waters,
patience was the deadliest weapon of all.
The attack wasn't a clash of equals. It was an ambush executed by a platform so
small
that standard anti-submarine sensors weren't calibrated to find it,
using a weapon so specific that its propulsion section could be identified by hand.
The North Koreans
thought the torpedo was untraceable. The wreck of ROKS Cheonan proved otherwise,
and the proof was sitting on the ocean floor
where they had left it.
On 20 May 2010,
the Joint Civilian-Military Investigation Group released its report. The JIG concluded that ROKS Cheonan was
sunk by
a North Korean torpedo,
fired from a North Korean midget submarine. The report cited the recovered propulsion section, the handwritten marking,
the
damage pattern on the wreck, and the torpedo fragments found in the debris field.
Pyongyang denied responsibility for the attack, as it had from
the first hours
after the sinking. The denial was total and public,
and North Korea demanded that South Korea allow its own investigators to
examine the evidence,
a request that Seoul rejected. Pyongyang argued that the JIG was a political instrument designed to justify
South Korean aggression,
and
it called for a new investigation led by neutral parties. The denial has never wavered,
and Pyongyang continues to reject the finding to this
day.
Inside South Korea,
a minority of academics raised questions about the JIG's analysis. Some pointed to inconsistencies in the report's
technical conclusions,
and
others questioned whether the evidence truly proved North Korean involvement beyond doubt. The JIG attributed its
findings to the physical evidence it had
gathered,
but the dissenting voices argued that the investigation had moved too quickly from explosion to attribution,
and that alternative explanations hadn't been fully
explored.
The dissenting academics noted that no direct electronic or acoustic contact with the submarine was ever established,
and that the JIG's conclusion relied
on circumstantial
and forensic evidence rather than real-time tracking. They argued that other explanations,
including an accidental collision with a submerged object or an
internal explosion triggered by a mine from
an earlier conflict,
deserved more scrutiny than the JIG gave them. These voices remained a minority in
South Korea,
but they were loud enough to keep the question alive in the public debate.
The world now had the evidence,
but the
question was whether the world wanted to act on it. The United Nations Security Council
responded on 9 July 2010 with Presidential Statement S/PRST/2010/13.
The statement condemned the attack that led to
the sinking of ROKS Cheonan,
but it didn't name North Korea as the perpetrator. The language
was careful,
reflecting the diplomatic reality that a direct attribution could escalate the crisis beyond the control of either
Korean state. The UN condemned
the attack,
the JIG attributed it to North Korea, and North Korea denied everything. The gap between forensic certainty
and diplomatic language remained open,
and the weapon that had signed its maker's name was still not enough to make the world
say it out loud.
The CHT-02D
torpedo was built to sink ships without a trace. Instead,
it signed its maker's name on the seabed. North Korea thought the weapon was
untraceable,
but the wreck of ROKS Cheonan proved that a handwritten marking can outlast a denial. If you
want to see how the next
crisis on the Korean peninsula unfolded, subscribe and stay with us.
